newsitem.title: USA: SEC told by lawmakers to rework derivatives rules.
newsitem.headline: SEC told by lawmakers to rework derivatives rules.

text.p: A Senate panel has asked the Securities and Exchange Commisson to go back to the drawing board, and re-work and test controversial rules requiring companies to disclose more information about the derivatives they own.
In a bi-partisan report sent to the agency late Monday, the Securities Subcommittee of the Senate Banking Committes told the SEC to delay using the new rules until they are improved.
"The application of the rules should be extended only after the Commission has carefully considered these results and made any changes," the Senate panel recommended in the report.
The panel has asked the agency to narrow the application of the rules to a smaller sample, use that as a pilot programme and draw up conclusions based on those trials, a Senate aide said.

Despite widespread opposition from companies and others, the SEC earlier this year approved its derivatives disclosure rules, which it wants to phase in during 1997 and 1998. The rules require companies to disclose the value of their derivatives holdings and any potential risks.
Most derivatives, financial instruments whose value is based on, or "derived from," the value of something else, are linked to interest rates or currencies.
Now the agency is left with little choice but to follow the lawmakers' recommendations since the rules face the threat of being overturned altogether.
An agency spokesman said the agency will respond quickly to the Senate report.
